description: Content Service operational dashboard — saturation, latency breakdown, failure modes. Drives load-test reads.

panels.description: Concurrent in-flight Fetch calls. Compare against GLOBAL_MAX_INFLIGHT (default 200) — when this gauge plateaus there, requests start queueing in the semaphore and queue time shows up as request latency. Previously every pod's "global" line (and every pod's "stream" line) rendered under the same identical legend text with no sum() — now split into a true aggregate per scope plus one line per pod (filterable via the Pod variable). GLOBAL_MAX_INFLIGHT (200) is a per-pod cap enforced independently by each pod's own semaphore, so compare the red line against the per-pod lines, not the total-across-pods line.
panels.title: In-flight requests (global vs stream)

panels.description:
Request rate split by status. Sustained 'failed' is the load-test failure signal.

Read this as per-DELIVERY outcomes, not per-document outcomes: a message that is Nak'd and redelivered counts once as a failure AND once as a completion if the retry succeeds (service.go, RecordRequest call site — documented in-code as intentional, true for every Nak path). This is why status lines often move together rather than partitioning total traffic cleanly: a burst of redeliveries raises delivery volume across every status at once, including `completed`, because each redelivery is counted as its own event. For the failure-reason breakdown of just the NATS lane, see 'NATS retry outcomes' below.
panels.title: Request rate by status

panels.description: End-to-end Fetch latency p50/p95/p99 across all api+content_type combinations.
panels.title: Request latency (p50/p95/p99)

panels.description: Rejections by reason. Non-zero = you've hit a concurrency ceiling. reason ∈ {global_full, stream_full, shutdown}.
panels.title: Rejections by reason

panels.description: Cache S3 op latency p99 split by op. Separates S3 latency from CS code paths. NOTE: since 2026-08 the read path serves hits HEAD-only (bodies are delivered via CacheLocation), so expect `get` volume to be a small fraction of `head` — a rising get rate means the extraction path or sha safety-net is doing the reading.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, bucket, op) (rate(content_cache_op_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m])))

panels.title: Cache op p99 latency (by bucket/op)

panels.description: NATS fetch outcomes per second by connector. outcome ∈ {completed, pickup_timeout, worker_timeout, canceled, error}. The *_timeout series are the load-test failure signals — non-zero pickup_timeout means connectors aren't keeping up; worker_timeout means they're stuck mid-fetch.
panels.title: NATS fetch outcomes by connector

panels.description:
Three separate ratios, not one "cache hit rate" — each answers a different question about a different code path, and they don't move together:

'Direct RAW request — served from cache' is the plain RAW-request path (phase=fetch): a drop here means RAW callers ('See Content', etc.) are increasingly hitting documents the cache doesn't have yet.

'TEXT request — raw already cached' is the raw-bucket check a TEXT request makes BEFORE it can extract (phase=extract): low/red here means TEXT requests are frequently paying for a connector round-trip before extraction can even start — the expensive path. This used to be silently merged into the RAW-request number above; it is now split out (NXS-2586 follow-up).

'TEXT request — text already cached' is whether the FINAL extracted output was already sitting in the text bucket — the cheapest possible outcome, no raw check or extraction needed at all.

A tile showing no data means that path has had zero traffic in the selected window, not a ratio of zero — e.g. an environment with no TEXT requests will never show either TEXT tile. A tile pinned red on a workload that fetches unique documents once (a first-pass bulk scan) is expected — there is nothing to hit yet, not a caching problem; a red tile on a workload that re-requests the same documents IS worth investigating.

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])) + sum(rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])))
targets.legendFormat: Direct RAW request — served from cache

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="extract"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="extract"}[5m])) + sum(rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="extract"}[5m])))

sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])) + sum(rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache hit ratio — by request type

panels.description: Text extraction p99 latency split by outcome. Only `success`/`failed` populate the histogram (skipped/breaker_open record duration=0 by design).

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, status) (rate(content_extraction_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m])))

panels.title: Extraction p99 latency (by status)

panels.description: NATS two-phase reply latency p99 by connector. pickup = publish → PROCESSING signal; worker = PROCESSING → COMPLETED reply. PICKUP_TIMEOUT and WORKER_TIMEOUT both default to 30s — sustained p99 climbing toward those thresholds means timeouts are imminent. Pairs with the NATS-outcomes panel.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, connector) (rate(content_nats_pickup_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, connector) (rate(content_nats_worker_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m])))

panels.title: NATS two-phase reply p99 (by connector)

panels.description: Cache write latency p50/p95/p99, SUCCESS ONLY — canceled/timeout are definitionally long-running (they measure how long a transfer ran before being abandoned) and poison the percentiles when mixed in; they have their own panel. Duration covers stream ingest + S3 upload but EXCLUDES the sha256 stamp copy (own panel). Buckets are explicit since 2026-08 — percentiles before that deploy were interpolation artifacts of the SDK's millisecond-scale defaults and read ~10-1000x too high.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[1m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[1m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[1m])))

panels.title: Cache write latency — success only (p50/p95/p99)

panels.description:
DISABLED — pending future work. content-service does not emit `content_extraction_circuit_state`, so this panel shows No data; there is no extractor circuit breaker in the service today. It is a placeholder for the breaker described in the xberg backpressure work, and will start working unchanged if that lands (the breaker is specified to report 0=closed / 1=half-open / 2=open, which the value mappings below already expect).

Until then, use `Retry attempts by error code` for extractor-saturation signal: a rising SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE line is xberg answering 503, which is what a breaker would trip on.
panels.title: Extractor circuit (DISABLED — pending breaker)

panels.description: S3 cache operation errors per second. error_type ∈ {read_failed, write_failed, other}.

targets.expr: sum by (bucket, op, error_type) (rate(content_cache_op_errors_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m]))

panels.title: Cache op errors (by error_type)

panels.description: Cache write outcomes from S3Store. result ∈ {success, read_error, size_mismatch, s3_error, canceled, timeout}. `timeout` = the CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS bound fired (was folded into `canceled` before 2026-08); `size_mismatch` now also deletes the truncated object.
panels.title: Cache write outcomes

panels.description: Requests FAILED during graceful shutdown drain. Should be zero except during deploy/restart.
panels.title: Shutdown-time failures

panels.description: sha256 safety-net activations — fires when the raw object carries no sha256 user-metadata (the stamp is written synchronously at cache-write time, so this should be ~zero outside legacy objects aging out of the 7d raw TTL). Steady non-zero `computed_in_process` = stamping regression; `raw_head_miss_text_hit` = text served after its raw was evicted AND the text object predates the sha stamp.
panels.title: sha256 safety-net activations

panels.description: Text extraction outcomes per second, status ∈ {success, failed, skipped, breaker_open}. If you see: `skipped` tracking near `success` — a large share of TEXT requests exceed EXTRACTION_MAX_SIZE (deployed: 50 MiB) and are served as raw bytes with no extraction attempted; check whether that's the expected corpus mix before assuming it's a problem. Sustained `breaker_open` — kreuzberg is sick and content-service has stopped sending it work; expect EXTRACTION_ERROR_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE to climb on the retry-attempts panel at the same time. Rising `failed` with flat `success` — documents are failing extraction outright (corrupt/unsupported content), not a capacity problem — compare against Retry attempts by error code to see which error is driving it. `success` alone tells you nothing about cost — pair with Extraction p99 latency to see if successes are getting slower.
panels.title: Extraction outcomes

panels.description: Distribution of bytes written per S3 cache Put — p50/p95/p99. Bodies above the transfer manager's 16 MiB multipart threshold take the multipart path. Useful for sizing payload-mix in load tests. 5m window deliberately wider than other panels — write events are infrequent and benefit from smoothing. Buckets are explicit (4KiB–5GiB) since 2026-08; earlier data used millisecond-scale defaults and is unreadable.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache write size distribution

panels.description: Splits successful raw-cache write latency into two views: `total p95` is the whole write (reading the connector's upload stream + the S3 PutObject), `stream-wait p95` is just the portion spent blocked reading bytes from the connector. total − stream-wait ≈ S3-side time. If `stream-wait` tracks close to `total`, the connector (its source system, e.g. Box/SharePoint) is the slow part, not the cache — do not chase S3 latency for that case. If `stream-wait` is small but `total` is high, S3 itself is slow.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_stream_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[5m])))

panels.title: Raw cache write p95 — time waiting on connector vs. total

panels.description: How long abandoned transfers ran before dying. `canceled` = the peer went away (connector crash, pod eviction, client deadline); `timeout` = the CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS bound fired. These are definitionally the long tail — kept OUT of the main latency panel so they can be read as what they are: client-abandonment behavior, not cache performance.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result=~"canceled|timeout"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache write — abandoned transfers (canceled/timeout)

panels.description: The post-upload sha256 metadata stamp (a server-side CopyObject self-copy, synchronous within Put but excluded from write-duration). Cost scales with object size — the copy rewrites the whole object, up to the 5GB CopyObject ceiling. Sustained `error` = objects left unstamped → sha safety-net activations downstream.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_sha_stamp_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))

panels.title: sha256 stamp (CopyObject) p95 by result

panels.description: Cache writes where the connector declared no size, so the post-upload byte-count validation was skipped — a client stream that died with a clean half-close mid-body is indistinguishable from a complete upload for these. Should be ~zero; any sustained rate means a connector is uploading unverifiable (possibly truncated) content.
panels.title: Unverified writes (no declared size)

panels.description: Upload streams currently admitted on the transfer listener. Each in-flight multipart upload holds ~48-64MiB of transfer-manager buffers; the uploadAdmission interceptor caps this service-wide at UPLOAD_MAX_CONCURRENT (default 32 — the red line). Sustained saturation = connectors are queueing behind the gate. Previously every pod's line rendered under the identical legend "in-flight uploads" with no sum() — now split into one true aggregate line plus one line per pod (filterable via the Pod variable).
panels.title: Upload streams in flight (cap 32)
Retry amplification — how one connector error becomes a platform stall (NXE-2480)

panels.description: Connector fetches issued per document actually drained by the privacy pipeline. 1.0 = healthy: every document fetched exactly once. The retry ladder is extractRetryMaxAttempts (5) × JetStream MaxDeliver (3) = 15, so a value approaching 15 means every failing document is consuming the whole ladder while holding one of the caller's workers. Measured 14.99 throughout the 2026-07-27 outage. NOTE: pii_* is emitted by the privacy job, so this reads true only while a privacy scan is running.
panels.title: Fetch amplification (fetches per document)

panels.description:
`failed_budget` is the one to read first — it is the common outcome now. The caller-wait budget (CALLER_WAIT_BUDGET_SECONDS, 5s) stops the in-handler retry ladder early, REPLIES to the caller so its worker is released, then Nak's with a 30s delay so the document is still retried. It was previously absent from this panel's query, which hid the majority of retry activity.

`failed` is a mixed bag: the two silent-Nak paths (in-handler attempts exhausted with deliveries left, and the request deadline firing) send NO reply, but a malformed request and a non-retryable manager failure also land here and DO reply. Treat a rising `failed` as "documents are being retried", not as "callers are stranded".

`failed_terminal` is the only outcome that both replies and Ack's — either MaxDeliver was reached or the budget was spent on the last allowed delivery. It is the end of the line for that document in this scan.

All three were EXACTLY 0.00/s during a clean S3-only window running at 87 completed/s, and ran sustained through the 2026-07-27 incident.

`failed_draining` was missing from this panel's filter (added) — a pod refusing to start new extraction work while shutting down, Nak'ing for a healthy replica to pick up (manager.go).

This panel tells you THAT a delivery was Nak'd and which of the four give-up reasons applied — it does NOT tell you the underlying connector/extraction error that caused it. The closest thing to a "why are we Naking" metric today is Retry attempts by error code (content_retry_attempts_total), but that counts in-handler retry attempts generally, including ones that go on to succeed without ever reaching a Nak — it is not scoped to "the attempt right before we gave up." The actual error code and message for a specific Nak are only in the Warn log line at the point of the decision ("service: retries exhausted, Nak'ing for JetStream redelivery" etc.), not in a metric label today.
panels.title: NATS retry outcomes — failed vs budget vs terminal vs draining (per delivery)

panels.description:
What to do: this should sit at ~0. If it's rising, requests are taking longer than the histogram can even measure (>60s) — every p95/p99 on this dashboard is being interpolated past its top bucket and UNDERSTATES the real tail, so don't trust those percentiles right now; go to Request latency and Extraction p99 latency to find which phase is stretching.

A sustained, near-constant (not spiky) non-zero value is the pattern seen during the 2026-07-27 outage: p95 pinned at exactly 29.00s for 360 consecutive samples — that's histogram interpolation lying, not a plateaued-but-fine service, because 100% of requests were stuck in the same (10s, 30s] bucket.

Why 60s: the service permits pickup 60s + worker 180s = 240s end-to-end, but content_request_duration_seconds' top explicit bucket stops at 60s — this panel is the only place that can see a request between 60s and the real 240s ceiling.

Gotcha if you edit this query: the bucket label is decimal-formatted (le="60.0"); le="60" silently matches nothing.

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", api="nats", le="+Inf"}[5m])) - sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", api="nats", le="60.0"}[5m]))

panels.title: Requests past the 60s top bucket

panels.description: Privacy document throughput against the rate below which its OpenSearch Point-in-Time lease expires. The reader paginates only as documents drain, and its consumers synchronise, so the gap between searches is 32 consumers × 1000-document pages ÷ throughput. Against a 30-minute lease that gives a critical rate of 32000/1800 = 17.8 docs/s. Sustained operation below the red line ends in a 404 search_context_missing_exception — and because the reader error is discarded at main.go:219, the scan then reports SUCCESS having read only part of the index. Requires a running privacy scan.
panels.title: Privacy throughput vs the PIT critical rate

panels.description:
Time a request spent waiting for an extraction slot before reaching xberg. This is the panel that separates "we queued" from "xberg was slow on this file" — without it both surface as the same error codes. Rising p95 here with `Extraction slots in use` pinned at capacity is a queueing problem, not a document problem. Buckets run to 600s because the extraction semaphore has no acquire timeout.

Split by lane, because that is the question the gate exists to answer. EXTRACTION_PRIORITY_MAX_CONSECUTIVE is wired so interactive extractions are not starved by pipeline ones, and undimensioned this panel shows the queue is deep without saying whether the requests waiting are the ones a human is waiting on. `interactive` climbing toward `bulk` means the priority lane is no longer buying anything.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))

panels.title: Extraction queue wait (admitted)

panels.description:
Occupancy of the extraction gate against EXTRACTION_MAX_CONCURRENCY (60 — the red line). That 60 is the DEPLOYED value, set under `contentService.env` in the applications chart; the code default is 10, so re-check the red line if dev retunes it. Occupancy SATURATES: once it is pinned it cannot tell you how far behind you are, which is what the queue-wait panel is for. `aborted/s` is requests whose deadline expired while queueing — sustained non-zero means the gate is shedding work rather than pacing it.

The total is kept as its own series because the red line applies to it, not to either lane alone. The per-lane split is what tells you who is holding the gate: `bulk` filling it during a scan is expected, but interactive extractions should still get in — read alongside `Extraction queue wait`, and note that slots held by extractions whose caller already left are counted in `Extractions that outlived their caller`.
panels.title: Extraction concurrency (cap 60) — slots occupied vs. requests that gave up waiting

panels.description:
What to do: a rising line here is a specific error driving repeated in-handler retries — the code name tells you where to look, not just that something's wrong.

EXTRACTION_ERROR_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE rising = kreuzberg is refusing work (likely overloaded); this is the amplification signal — content-service retrying a busy extractor 3x per delivery across multiple deliveries makes the backlog worse, not better. EXTRACTION_ERROR_TIMEOUT = documents are genuinely slow to extract; capped at fewer attempts than other codes because a document that timed out once will very likely time out again. CONTENT_ERROR_CACHE_WRITE_FAILED = the connector's write into our raw cache is failing — check S3/cache health, not the extractor. CONTENT_ERROR_INTERNAL here specifically means the connector couldn't reach or was rate-limited by the SOURCE system (Box/SharePoint/etc.) — a source-side problem, not a content-service one.
panels.title: Retry attempts by error code

panels.description:
How a connector's Fetch attempt failed, one line per (code, retryable). Use `code` to jump from an error spike back to the URNs causing it. `retryable=true` means content-service will try this document again automatically — `retryable=false` means it won't, so a rising non-retryable line is documents that need a human or a source-side fix, not a wait-it-out situation.

CACHE_WRITE_FAILED is always retryable regardless of what the connector reports — a failed write to our own S3 cache is treated as transient. TOO_LARGE is essentially never retryable — the source object is over the connector's size limit, and that won't change on the next attempt. CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE means no connector answered our reply inbox within PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS — it does NOT mean the request was lost, it stays queued on CONTENT_FETCH and will be picked up.
panels.title: Connector fetch errors by code

panels.description:
Valkey claims taken before a connector fetch or an xberg extraction, so two replicas don't do the same work. Expect everything but `won` to sit at zero until KEDA scales past one replica.

`won` — this pod took the claim and is doing the work.
`lost` — another replica holds it, so this one waits for the output instead.
`preempted` — interactive work took a bulk holder's claim. A DELIBERATE duplicate: the displaced holder keeps working, so for a window two replicas do the same work. That is the price of putting a human ahead of a scan, and it is a separate label so the price is visible rather than folded into `won`.
`held_by_self` — this pod found its OWN earlier claim, almost always a fetch claim retained past a reply timeout. No peer is involved and the work is at a connector. Split out of `lost` on purpose: counted as a cross-pod loss, a connector slowdown on one pod read as a dedup success story.
`duplicated` — gave up waiting and did the work anyway knowing a peer holds the claim. Only interactive requests do this, because a synchronous call has no redelivery to defer to. Buys a full duplicate.
`lease_lost` — a renewal found the claim gone while the work was still running: it lapsed, or an interactive claimant preempted it. This is the LEADING INDICATOR of duplicate work.
`unavailable` — Valkey is unreachable and dedup has silently degraded. Everything still works, it just costs duplicate fetches and extractions.
`disabled` — dedup is not running at all for that phase: VALKEY_HOST unset, or that phase's marker TTL zeroed. Emitted deliberately so "dedup is off" is visible; an absent series looks identical to no traffic. With both TTLs set and Valkey wired, this should be flat zero.

The two worth watching are `disabled` (off by configuration, a likelier regression than an outage) and `lease_lost` (duplicate work is now happening).
panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — claim outcomes

panels.description:
What to look for: a rising `peer`/`satisfied` line is dedup actually paying off — another replica held the claim and this request waited instead of repeating a connector fetch or xberg run. A rising `connector` line is NOT dedup — it means this request holds its OWN claim and its own reply from the connector timed out, so read `connector` volume as connector slowness, not a dedup signal (reading it as dedup overstates the payoff by exactly that many reply timeouts). A rising `took_over` is the one to escalate: the previous claim holder stopped renewing with nothing written (it died mid-work), and this request discovered that and redid the work itself — a steady trickle is normal pod recycling, a spike means replicas are dying under load.

Why the two sources move independently: `peer` scales with replica count and hot keys (many pods racing the same document), `connector` scales with source-system load (Box/SharePoint/etc. being slow) — they are not substitutes for each other. `extract` is always `peer`, never `connector`, because an extraction is synchronous work with no dispatched request that could outlive our own timeout the way a connector fetch can.

Any non-`satisfied` outcome means the request did the work itself rather than reusing someone else's — that is a missed optimization, never a failure; the wait can only save effort, not cause one. `skipped` specifically means there was no deadline left to wait within at all (PEER_WAIT_SECONDS/CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS bound the wait itself, GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS bounds both) — a high `skipped` rate next to a flat `satisfied` rate is a timing-budget problem, not a dedup problem, and retuning those seconds is the fix, not investigating the claim logic. `expired` (someone is still working, we gave up waiting) and `took_over` (nobody was working, we found out) look identical in wall-clock terms but mean opposite things — don't conflate them.

targets.expr: sum by (phase, source, outcome) (rate(content_dedup_waits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m]))

panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — work avoided vs redone

panels.description:
How long a wait took before it paid off, split by who we waited on. Filtered to outcome="satisfied" on purpose: an expired wait always equals its whole budget, so including it would flatten every quantile onto the ceiling and say nothing. Which budget depends on who we waited on — PEER_WAIT_SECONDS bounds a peer wait, CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS a connector one, and GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS caps both. They are the same number in dev today only because PEER_WAIT_SECONDS is not templated into the configmap and inherits the connector value. Read with `Cross-pod dedup — work avoided vs redone`, which gives the counts these durations belong to.

`fetch/peer` is how long a follower waits for the replica holding the claim — it tracks connector latency plus whatever was left of the holder's lease when we joined. `fetch/connector` is how far past our own reply timeout the connector actually ran, which is the number to size PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and the worker timeout against. `extract/peer` is how long another replica's xberg run took to land.

p50 and p95 only, since splitting by phase and source already yields three series per quantile. Buckets run to 600s (cacheWriteBuckets), so waits longer than that are unresolvable — but the wait budget is well under it, so that ceiling should never bind.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — how long a paying wait took

panels.description:
Extractions that finished after the caller had already gone. This is DELIBERATE, not a leak: cancelling a POST to xberg mid-flight throws the whole run away, because nothing is persisted until the extractor returns. Carrying on means the caller's retry finds the text cached and pays for a HEAD instead of a second full run.

What it costs is an extraction slot held for work nobody is waiting on, which is why it is counted here rather than left to be inferred from queue depth. Read it against `Extraction slots in use`: a rising count while the gate is pinned means part of your capacity is committed to callers who have left, and the queue behind it is waiting on them.

A steady low rate is the design working — bulk requests hit their delivery deadline and retry into the cache. Sustained `interactive` is worse than sustained `bulk`: a human gave up waiting, and the deadline is doing the abandoning rather than the extractor being slow, so check GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS against the extraction phase before tuning anything else.
panels.title: Extractions that outlived their caller
KEDA inflight trigger — baseline before retuning the threshold
What the autoscaler sees vs what is really in flight
panels.description:
The KEDA trigger runs sum(content_inflight_global) with NO label filter, so it is the series to read before changing contentService.autoscaling.triggers.inflight.threshold (default 100) or activationThreshold (default 20).

Two things inflate it against the job-filtered series below it.

1. Dual scrape. Every app metric in eks-integration is scraped twice, by job="kubernetes-services" and by the PodMonitor job, both reporting identical values — so an unfiltered sum() counts each pod twice. The three NATS triggers use max(), which is idempotent under that duplication; this trigger is the only one using sum(), so it is the only one affected.

2. No namespace filter. If this Prometheus serves more than one namespace, they are all in the KEDA number and none of them are in $namespace.

Divide the KEDA series by the threshold to get the replicas this trigger asks for. KEDA takes the highest count any trigger requests, so this one can only ever raise the count the queue triggers ask for.

panels.title: Replicas this trigger is asking for
panels.description: ceil(KEDA query / threshold), clamped to maxReplicas (default 5). Red at 5 means the trigger is pinned at the ceiling, where it can no longer distinguish "full" from "far behind" — the state to avoid when picking a new threshold. The admission gate refuses work past globalMaxInflight (deployed 200) per pod, so the gauge has a hard ceiling of its own.

panels.title: Is there any See Content load to scale on?
panels.description:
content_inflight_global carries no scope label, so the gauge cannot be split into NATS vs gRPC. Request rate by api is the closest proxy: grpc_get_content and grpc_fetch_stream are See Content, nats is the scan lane.

This is the traffic that was never counted in the gauge before the IncInflight scope fix. If these series are flat zero, the threshold does not need to move at all — nothing new is being added to the sum.

panels.title: TEXT vs RAW — cache path (NXS-2586 follow-up)

panels.description:
Where a request's bytes actually came from, split by request type. Read it as: rising 'text already cached' = TEXT requests answered with zero backend work. Rising 'raw already cached, extracted fresh' alongside a flat/low 'raw not cached' = TEXT misses are cheap — extraction only, no connector round-trip. Rising 'raw not cached' = TEXT requests paying for a connector fetch AND an extraction, the most expensive path — if this climbs during an incident, the raw cache is not doing its job for TEXT traffic specifically. The two 'direct RAW request' lines are the same question for plain RAW requests, which never run extraction at all.

Caveat: a text-cache miss is recorded once per incoming request, but the raw-bucket check underneath it is deduplicated across concurrent requests for the same document (singleflight) — so during a concurrent burst on one URN, 'text already cached'-miss count and the two raw lines below it are not guaranteed to add up 1:1.
